title: How Dolphins Work!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore dolphins, focusing on bottlenose dolphins: their classification as cetaceans, evolutionary origins from pakicetus, placental reproduction and nursing, anatomy (blowhole, melon, pectoral fins, flukes, vestigial ears, earwax layers), eyesight, echolocation, sound production, intelligence and tool use, social pods and behavior including altruism and non-conceptive sexual behavior, the Peter and Margaret Howe Lovatt experiment with John C. Lilly, captivity and dolphin entertainment, US Navy marine mammal program, dolphin deaths and hunts in Taiji and the Faroe Islands, bycatch and tuna labeling, and US Marine Mammal Protection Act. Episode ends with listener mail about a VW Lemon ad and a correction to the Zizians episode concerning Eliezer Yudkowsky and the Machine Intelligence Research Institute.

segments.title: Opening banter and chassis correction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show with banter, including a pronunciation correction about the word chassis.

segments.title: What dolphins are and which ones are discussed
segments.summary: Dolphins are cetaceans, a marine mammal group with about eighty related species including whales and porpoises. There are over forty dolphin species in the oceanic family and four river dolphin species. The episode focuses mainly on bottlenose dolphins.

segments.title: Lifespan and dolphins near shore
segments.summary: Bottlenose dolphins live about 45 to 50 years in the wild, with a disputed shorter captive lifespan discussed later. Common dolphins tend to stay closer to shore, and the hosts discuss dolphins they saw near a lagoon.

segments.title: Evolution from land mammals to dolphins
segments.summary: Dolphins descended from Pakicetus, a wolf-sized four-legged land mammal about fifty million years ago. Dolphins are more closely related to hippos than to sea lions or otters. Embryonic dolphins briefly develop limbs.

segments.title: Reproduction and nursing
segments.summary: Dolphins are placental mammals that bear live young after pregnancies of about ten to eighteen months. Orcas, which are dolphins, have the longest gestation at about eighteen months. Calves nurse for up to two years and stay with mothers for years. Dolphins nurse underwater by rolling the tongue into a straw shape.

segments.title: Dolphin milk taste
segments.summary: Lilian Eichelberger reportedly tasted dolphin milk in 1940 and described it as fishy, oily, and lacking sweetness.

segments.title: Swimming, fins, blubber and tail anatomy
segments.summary: Dolphins are streamlined and swim often. Pectoral fins made of cartilage steer, the dorsal fin provides stability, and horizontal flukes move the tail up and down. Blubber provides buoyancy, insulation, and an energy reserve.

segments.title: Porpoising and the Weapons movie tangent
segments.summary: Dolphins leap in and out of the water, a behavior called porpoising, which penguins also do. The hosts briefly discuss the movie Weapons.

segments.title: Blowhole, breathing and spout
segments.summary: The blowhole connects directly to the lungs and can be opened and closed with a nasal plug. Dolphins breathe five or six times a minute and can hold their breath for a few minutes. They are air-breathing mammals and cannot drown in the usual sense. The spout forms as warm breath condenses in cold air.

segments.title: Unihemispheric sleep
segments.summary: Dolphins sleep with one brain hemisphere at a time, keeping the other alert to avoid predators and keep swimming. The hosts link this to the Zizians episode.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break between segments.

segments.title: Dolphin eyesight
segments.summary: Dolphins have two eyes on the sides of the head giving nearly 300-degree panoramic vision with a blind spot above. Their double-slit pupils adjust to light, and they can see up to about 150 feet.

segments.title: Teeth, diet and feeding
segments.summary: Dolphins have cone-shaped teeth and eat fish, crustaceans, and squid. They swallow prey headfirst and can bite off spiny heads of fish like catfish.

segments.title: Hearing, earwax layers and echolocation hearing
segments.summary: Dolphins have vestigial ear canals plugged with earwax. Earwax layers can be examined like tree rings to estimate age and reveal pollutants and hormone changes. Dolphins hear high-frequency sound through their lower jaw and acoustic fats.

segments.title: Sonar harm and Arabian Sea strandings
segments.summary: Naval sonar harms dolphins. In 2009, about two hundred dolphins stranded during a multinational naval exercise in the Arabian Sea.

segments.title: Vocalizations, phonic lips, larynx and melon
segments.summary: Dolphins make whistles, pops, and brays using phonic lips near the blowhole and a larynx. The melon, a fatty forehead structure, focuses sound like a lens.

segments.title: Signature whistles and baby talk
segments.summary: Dolphins use signature whistles to identify themselves and locate each other. Mothers use higher-frequency baby talk with calves.

segments.title: Echolocation
segments.summary: Dolphins use echolocation, convergent with bats, producing clicks focused by the melon and building a mental map from returning echoes. Studies show they distinguish disc sizes differing by one tenth of a centimeter. They can reportedly see internal organs of other animals.

segments.title: Predator movie tangent
segments.summary: Brief tangent about the Predator movies and the Alien universe after the mention of heat-based vision.

segments.title: Dolphin pods and social structure
segments.summary: Dolphin pods range from two to a thousand, usually forty to sixty. Pod types include juvenile pods, bachelor pods, and family pods, with advantages for hunting, defense, and passing knowledge.

segments.title: Male coalitions, abduction of females, and altruism
segments.summary: Males sometimes team up to steal and keep a female from another pod, since females are unavailable to breed during long gestation and lactation. Dolphins also show altruism, such as a group of eleven dolphins supporting an injured companion in the mid-2000s.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Second break between segments.

segments.title: Play, teasing, and sexual behavior
segments.summary: Dolphins play, tease fish, and porpoise in ship wakes for thrills. Male bachelor pods form lifelong friendships and show non-conceptive sexual behavior. Captive dolphins are reported to engage in masturbation, including using objects.

segments.title: Dolphin intelligence, John C. Lilly, and Peter and Margaret Howe Lovatt
segments.summary: John C. Lilly in the 1960s argued dolphins were nearly as intelligent as humans, and conducted invasive experiments. In 1963 he paired a woman, Margaret Howe Lovatt, with a dolphin named Peter in a flooded apartment. The project ended when funding dried up, Peter was separated from Margaret, and he died by sinking to the bottom and not breathing.

segments.title: Dolphin intelligence debate and tool use
segments.summary: Hosts argue against comparing animal intelligence to humans. Some bottlenose dolphins use sponges as tools while foraging, learned within pods, which fits criteria for culture.

segments.title: Captivity, dolphin entertainment and mortality
segments.summary: Dolphin entertainment dates to the 1800s and grew after the TV show Flipper in the 1960s. Mortality rates in captivity are disputed between SeaWorld research and former employees. A 1988 study found about half of captive dolphins die within ninety days of capture. SeaWorld stopped breeding orcas in 2016 after Blackfish. Critics say captive research distorts behavior.

segments.title: US Navy marine mammal program and Tiaw
segments.summary: The US Navy started its Marine Mammal Program in 1959 and uses dolphins to find mines and track swimmers. A dolphin named Tiaw killed a man in Brazil in 1994.

segments.title: Dolphin watching and boat impacts
segments.summary: Dolphin watching can disturb dolphins, especially with feeding, too many boats, and collisions. Responsible operators follow time and distance limits.

segments.title: US laws and dolphin-safe tuna
segments.summary: The Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972 bans eating dolphin in the US. Dolphin-safe tuna labels such as pole caught and troll caught reduce bycatch risk.

segments.title: Chicken of the Sea tangent
segments.summary: Light conversation about Chicken of the Sea tuna and a reality TV show, with Chuck and Josh talking about past viewing.

segments.title: Dolphin drive hunts and bycatch statistics
segments.summary: Drive hunts in Taiji, Japan and the Faroe Islands kill dolphins; The Cove and Sea Spiracy document them. A 2020 study estimated large bycatch in the Indian Ocean. Ghost fishing gear also kills marine life.

segments.title: Closing thoughts on dolphins
segments.summary: Josh recaps dolphin mothers using whistles for baby talk and dolphins playing, then transitions to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: VW Lemon ad
segments.summary: A listener named Lori, an advertising copywriter, explains the VW Lemon ad: the car had a scratch on the glove compartment and fine print explained that. The insight for the VW Beetle is that you don't buy a Beetle, you adopt it.

segments.title: Correction: Zizians episode and Eliezer Yudkowsky
segments.summary: Josh corrects the Zizians episode: Eliezer Yudkowsky did not throw in the towel. His forthcoming book If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies argues there is still time to build friendly AI. The correction came from Malo Borgan, CEO of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh close with contact information and the show's credits.
